idiom_name: container or framework enforcement point (AuthorizationManager behind an AuthorizationFilter) plus a final decision class
implementation_notes: Java's own reference monitor - the Security Manager with AccessController.checkPermission, which walked the call stack and threw unless every protection domain held the permission, with java.security.Policy holding the rules - is deprecated for removal (JEP 411) and permanently disabled in JDK 24 (JEP 486): enabling it is a startup error, System.setSecurityManager throws an UnsupportedOperationException, and the JEP states explicitly that no replacement is promised. What remains is the library realization: an enforcement point that runs on every request or every method, such as Spring Security's AuthorizationFilter feeding an AuthorizationManager that matches the request and runs the rule, denying by default and delegating to an external policy agent when the rules live elsewhere. The small verifiable core is then a final class with private fields that owns no policy logic and calls a replaceable store, while tamper resistance is accepted to be a deployment property - the JEP's own advice is containers, hypervisors and OS sandboxing.
pitfalls: Reflection (setAccessible), java.lang.instrument agents and --add-opens reach private and final members, so the class is a reviewable core rather than a tamperproof one; hostile code is stopped by the container or OS sandbox.

The retired mechanism must not be re-implemented by hand: installing a custom SecurityManager is an error on JDK 24 and no supported equivalent exists, so code that relied on it needs a framework enforcement point or an out-of-process boundary.

Principal propagation is manual: an Authentication bound to a request thread is lost in executors and asynchronous stages unless it is re-bound and cleared per task, and a stale binding makes the monitor decide for the previous caller.

Framework rule sets permit by default (anyRequest().permitAll(), or endpoints registered outside the filter chain): completeness is lost in configuration, not in code, so the rule list needs its own review.
